resources.string: We could not find any history for this website. Real banks and government services have used their websites for many years.
This website was created only %1$s days ago. Real banks and government services have used their websites for many years.
This link goes to %1$s, which is made to look like the real %2$s website. The real address is %3$s.
The web address %1$s uses letters that look like normal English letters but are not. This is a common trick to fool your eyes.
The link %1$s is a shortened link. We cannot see where it actually leads before you tap it.
The message shows the address %1$s, but the link actually goes to %2$s instead.
This link goes straight to a set of numbers (%1$s) instead of a normal web address. Real banks and services do not do this.
The web address ends in .%1$s, an ending that is often used for fake websites.
This link is not secured, and it asks for details like a password or OTP. A genuine bank page would not ask this way.
This message claims to be from a company, but it did not come from a verified business number.
This message claims to be from a company, but it came from an ordinary 10-digit mobile number, not a verified business number.
This message claims to be from %1$s, but it was actually sent using a business number registered to %2$s.
This message asks you to share an OTP, PIN, or CVV. No genuine bank or company ever asks for this.
This message talks about approving a payment request to \"receive\" money. Approving a UPI request always sends money out, never in.
This message pushes you to act right now, before you have time to think it over. That pressure is a common scam tactic.
This message threatens that something bad will happen — your account blocked, your power cut, or legal action — unless you act immediately.
This message promises a prize, lottery, or reward that is too good to be true, especially since you never entered anything.
This message includes a number that may charge you extra just for calling or texting it.
This message includes a cryptocurrency wallet address. Genuine banks and services never ask for payment this way.
This message asks you to pay a fee first, before you can receive a job, prize, or loan. Genuine offers never work this way.
Our on-device model finds this message very similar to known scam messages.
Our on-device model finds this message similar to ordinary, genuine messages.
Do not enter your bank or KYC details on this link.
Genuine employers never ask you to pay to get hired.
You cannot win a lottery or contest you never entered.
No police officer or government agency arrests anyone over a phone call or video call.
Genuine courier and customs fees are never collected by asking you to click a link and pay online.
Be careful with loan apps that ask for large permissions on your phone or an upfront fee before lending anything.
Never approve a UPI request from someone you do not know. Approving it sends your money to them.
Be very cautious of investment plans that promise guaranteed or unusually high returns.
A genuine company will never call you out of the blue asking for remote access to your device.
Do not pay. Do not respond. Save the evidence and report it.
Contact your electricity board directly using the number on a past bill, not a number from this message.
Do not act on this message until you have checked it another way.
Do not click any link in this message.
Never share an OTP, PIN, or CVV with anyone, even someone who says they are calling from your bank.
If you want to check, call the number printed on your bank card or bill — not any number from this message.
You can report this at cybercrime.gov.in or by calling 1930.
